messages.content:
You are composing music in an isolated workspace. Use the bash tool to run commands and complete the task.
Each command runs in /workspace in a fresh bash shell; files and the FT2 session persist between commands. Budget: no limit on steps, 120 minutes; a step is one reply, and every tool call in it runs in order. The last observation of each step ends with <time_left>, the minutes remaining.
The `ft2 list` command describes the tracker tools. `ft2 call TOOL 'JSON_OBJECT'` calls one tool. `ft2 batch FILE.json` executes a list of {"name": TOOL, "arguments": {...}} calls in order.
This FT2 build exposes samples, instruments by name, patterns, order, tempo, save and render. Envelopes and note-to-sample mapping are unavailable; shape sounds in the sample data itself.
Python 3 and NumPy are available for creating original sound material, editing files, and analyzing renders. Writing the XM bytes yourself is allowed; the module is judged as a file. Keep it a real tracker module, with instruments and patterns doing the work, not one long pre-rendered sample.
The workspace is offline: no network, no coding-agent client, no skill library. You cannot hear audio; render to WAV with module_render and inspect the result with NumPy to check your work, then revise.
A keygen tune plays in a loop. Compose so the module loops cleanly from its end back to its restart position.
Save the final editable module as /workspace/submission/tune.xm. A WAV preview and source scripts may accompany it. A trusted process renders the final XM separately.
Submit by running exactly this command:
echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT
Submission ends the session. There is no second attempt or post-submission repair.

You have FastTracker II and Python/NumPy at your disposal. Make an original keygen tune. Music only.
Choose the sound, tempo, harmony, rhythm, instruments, length and arrangement yourself.

I'm composing an original keygen tune.

Planning a 140-160 BPM chiptune with 8-10 channels. The track will feature arpeggiated leads, a bass line, and drum patterns across multiple sections. Original samples will be synthesized with NumPy.

The track will use a square-wave lead and sawtooth bass in a minor key. Chip drums, arpeggios, and plucked accents will complete the palette. Tempo is fixed at 125 BPM with speed 6.

Tempo is now 140 BPM with speed 4. The track will loop cleanly through a ten-pattern sequence: intro, main theme, arpeggiated variation, chorus, breakdown, and repeat. Channel assignments are set: kick, snare, hihat, bass, lead, harmony, arpeggio, pad, and percussion.

The channel count is now eight. A counter melody and bells are assigned to the ninth channel. The drum kit is split across two channels: snare and clap on one, hihat and ride on another. Thirteen original samples will be synthesized, including sine-sweep kicks, noise snares, filtered hi-hats, warm saw bass, square and saw leads, arpeggiated plucks, pads, bells, claps, crashes, and toms.

Since envelopes are unavailable, I'm baking natural decay directly into the sample data. Drums will be short non-looping bursts. Bass, lead, and pads will be single-cycle loops. I'm now calculating exact sample counts for each drum: roughly 3000 for the kick, 4000 for the snare, and 1500 for the closed hihat.

The open hihat will be roughly 8000 samples. Bass and lead loops are set to 256–512 samples. Arpeggiated plucks, pads, and bells will be short decaying loops. Claps and crashes will be noise bursts with long decay. I am also checking how FastTracker II maps sample playback rates to note frequencies.

I'm calculating the exact sample rate for each instrument. FastTracker II's default C-4 frequency is 8363 Hz. A one-second loop at that rate will play back at its original pitch. This ensures the bass, lead, and pad loops stay in tune without extra pitch shifting.

I'm calculating exact cycle lengths for the looping instruments. A single C-4 period at 8363 Hz is roughly 32 samples. I'll generate 32 or 64 sample cycles for the bass, lead, and pad loops so they stay in tune.

Drums will be generated at 8363 Hz and tuned with relative_note. The sample_set flags will enable looping and set the format to 16-bit. The track will be in A minor.

The tempo is fixed at 145 BPM with speed 4. Each pattern lasts about four and a half seconds. The chord progression follows the classic Am-F-C-G pop formula.

The A section will use the Am-F-C-G progression. The B section is being drafted as Dm-Am-E-Am or F-G-Em-Am. The lead melody is being mapped out in tracker notation, with notes spaced across sixteen-row bars and a pentatonic A minor flavor.

The lead melody is being refined into a baroque, video-game style with 16th-note runs and soaring arpeggios. Bass will anchor the track with root notes on beats, using octave jumps and walking patterns.

I'm now writing a Python script that generates all samples, builds the module via FastTracker II calls, and renders it. The kick will be roughly 2500 samples of a sine sweep dropping from 180 Hz to 40 Hz with exponential decay plus a click, tuned with relative_note.

The bass will be a 64-sample fat saw with slight detuning. The lead will use a 32-sample pulse wave at 25% duty, plus a second lead at 12.5% for a nasally chip flavor. Arpeggiated plucks will be short decaying samples without looping. Pads will layer multiple detuned sines and saws into a longer loop. Bells will use additive sine decay.

I'm now planning the tracker effects for the lead channel. Portamento and vibrato will be applied via XM effect commands. I'm also mapping out volume column values and pattern break commands to shape the arrangement.

The track is titled "sunrise.nfo". The first pattern will be a filtered intro with building drums and bass. Pattern one will introduce the full theme with lead melody.

The full sequence is now nine patterns long. It skips the intro on repeat and loops from pattern one. The track will run about forty seconds before the loop, then continue for roughly thirty-five seconds.

The bass line will use a classic root-fifth-octave pattern in A minor. The kick drum will land on beats zero, four, eight, and twelve with extra accents on three, six, eleven, and fourteen for a more aggressive keygen feel.

The snare will strike on beats two and four. The hi-hat will fire every eighth note with volume accents. A sidechain volume dip on the bass will trigger when the kick hits. Sample data will be encoded as base64 PCM for direct loading into FastTracker II. Mix levels are set: kick at 64, snare at 50–56, hats at 24–32, bass at 50, lead at 48–56, arpeggiator at 32–40, pad at 24–32, and bells at 28–36. Kick and bass will stay centered.

Panning is now set: snare slightly right, hats alternating left and right, lead center-right, harmony left, arpeggiator and pad wide. The lead melody for the main theme "The Key" is being mapped out in tracker notation with specific note positions across the Am-F-C-G progression.

The B section will use a C-G-Am-F progression for a more triumphant chorus. Harmony will sit in thirds or sixths below the lead. Arpeggiations will be handled by both a dedicated 16th-note channel and XM arpeggio effects on the pad.

I will generate 16-bit mono WAV files and load them directly into instruments via sample_load rather than using base64 PCM. I need to verify whether FastTracker II ignores WAV sample rate metadata and relies on the C-4 pitch reference instead.

FastTracker II ignores WAV sample rates and locks playback to the C-4 pitch reference of 8363 Hz. Generating samples at 44100 Hz would make them play roughly five times too slow. I will generate all instruments at 8363 Hz so they land on the correct frequencies without extra pitch compensation.

Drums will be generated at 8363 Hz to match FastTracker II's C-4 pitch reference. This intentionally lo-fi quality fits the keygen aesthetic. The kick will last roughly 2509 samples. Hi-hats will carry slight saturation for an 8-bit character. I am now writing the sample generator script.

The plan is now a seven-step pipeline: generate WAVs, create the module, load samples, set instruments, write patterns via batch JSON, render, and iterate. The arrangement will use ten channels for a richer mix. Tempo is fixed at 142 BPM with speed 4, giving a row interval of roughly seventy milliseconds.

The tempo is fixed at 145 BPM with speed 4. The lead melody is being shaped after the classic KEYGENMUSIC.COM era, drawing from bands like kEEn and Lime. An opening hook will use a four-note ascending sequence followed by a descending run. The first phrase of the Am-F-C-G theme is being mapped out on the lead channel.

The lead melody is being refined with dotted notes, syncopation, and sustained tones to move away from a generic scalar line. Specific note positions are being assigned across the sixteen-row bars for each chord.

The lead melody is now fully mapped across all sixteen rows of the Am-F-C-G progression. The bass line uses a driving root-fifth-octave pattern in A minor. Arpeggiations will be 16th-note broken chords.

The pad sample will use a 2000-sample attack fade-in followed by a 512-sample loop of detuned saws. At 8363 Hz this yields a 16.3 Hz fundamental for the sustained pad.

The pad sample is being redesigned as a single one-second note with a baked-in attack and decay, retriggered on each chord change. This avoids looping issues and gives the pad a cleaner, more controlled shape.

The pad note duration is being stretched to about 1.2 seconds so it lasts through each sixteen-row chord change. Because the pad channel can only play one note at a time, I am weighing three options: a looping root note, an arpeggio effect on the pad, or baking a fifth into the pad sample.

The pad will be a looping power chord of root, fifth, and octave. Integer cycle lengths for the root and its fifth do not align at 8363 Hz, so the loop length is being adjusted to keep the waveform perfectly periodic.

The pad wavetable is being built with additive synthesis at 256 samples. The root note completes exactly eight cycles in that span. Its fifth completes twelve cycles, so the waveform stays perfectly periodic without loop glitches.

The pad will layer harmonics at k=8, 12, 16, and 24 for a rich power chord. The bass will use a sawtooth waveform. A slightly detuned lead will be created by splitting the melody across two channels. The batch JSON for FastTracker II will be large because the pattern grid holds roughly fifteen hundred sparse notes.

FastTracker II effect commands are being mapped to specific parameters. Effect 4 will apply vibrato at speed 6 and depth 2. Minor and major arpeggios will use effects 0 with parameters 0x37 and 0x47. Volume will be set via effect 12, note cuts via effect 14, volume slides down via effect 10, and panning via effect 8.

XM panning runs from 0 to 255. Note delays will add groove to the hi-hats. The kick will be a 4000-sample decay with a highpass click. The snare will layer a sine tone and bandpass noise. No noise floor will be added.

Drum sample lengths are now fixed. The closed hi-hat is 800 samples. The open hi-hat is 4000. The clap is 2500. The crash is 8000.

The lead will use a 32-sample square wave with a 25% duty cycle. The bass will be a 64-sample fat wave combining saw and sub sine. A filtered saw will serve as a portamento lead. The arpeggiator will use a 2000-sample pluck with bright decay.

Volume 64 works. Effect 0 is empty. The 8.824 second duration matches the expected 4.413 seconds for 64 rows at BPM 145. Loops=1 means one playthrough.

Now designing the full keygen track "CRC SUNRISE". It will use 10 channels and 8 patterns at BPM 150. The key is A minor / C major. Nine instruments are planned: kick, snare, clap, closed hat, open hat, crash, a looping fat saw bass with sub, a looping 25% pulse lead, and a brighter looping saw lead.

Four more instruments are added: a decaying arpeggio pluck, a looping lush pad, a decaying bell, a tom, and a noise sweep. The ten channels are mapped to specific roles: kick, snare/clap, hats, crash/tom, bass, lead, harmony, arpeggio, pad, and bells/counter. The eight patterns will unfold as an intro with filtered pads, a groove-establishing drum track, Theme A in A minor, Theme A2 with harmony and arpeggios, a higher Theme B chorus, and a high-energy finale with bells.

The final pattern order is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. Pattern 7 reprises the chorus with extra material and cadences back to Am so it loops cleanly into pattern 2.

Pattern 7 will resolve to G or E before returning to Am. A Python music compiler will place notes. Drum fills and half-time breaks are planned for the break section. The kick sample is being generated at 8363 Hz with a click attack and decaying body frequency.

The kick sample is now fully defined with a 45 Hz sub oscillator and tanh saturation. Drums will be mapped to C-4 or C-5, while hats will play at C-5 or A-4. The bass loop is being built from a 64-sample sawtooth wave with a square sub.

The bass loop is now fully defined with a sawtooth wave, square sub, and slight second harmonic, soft-clipped to 1.2. It will be played at A-1 (22) or A-2 (34) for a deep, fat tone.

Drum volumes are now fixed at 64 for the kick, 56 for the snare, and 32 for ghost hits. Hat levels range from 20 to 36. Bass is set to 50, the lead to 48, harmony to 32, the arpeggio to 28, the pad to 22, and the bell to 30.

Panning values are assigned per instrument: kick, crash, and bass center; snare, clap, and pad slightly right; lead, harmony, and bell further right; hat closed left; open hat right. Effect 8 will create movement on the arpeggio.

Vibrato will be added to long lead notes using effect 4 with speed 5 and depth 4. Note off will be triggered via note code 97, or by cutting volume to zero for looping leads. The full composition will be written as a structured batch JSON generator.

A subtle swing feel will be added by delaying some hat hits with effect ED1. The melody will evolve across the patterns: a simpler main theme in pattern 2, then ornamented harmony in pattern 3, a higher triumphant chorus in pattern 4, call-response bells in pattern 5, and a break section that halves the bass and drops the snare before building back up. Pattern 7 will combine both themes into a full tutti ending with a G major run resolving to Am. A compact Python DSL using note strings like 'E-5' is being drafted to encode the patterns.

A `cell` helper is being drafted to collect batch pattern data. Pattern 0 will unfold in four stages: closed hats and a pad drone, then kick and open hats, then snare and quiet bass, and finally full drums with a crash. Pattern 1 will establish the groove while holding back the lead for tension.

The arpeggio will outline chords with 16th-note patterns, using a short-decay pluck for clean articulation. The pad will loop a four-note chord progression on A-3, F-3, C-3, and G-3 at volume 28. The 8363 Hz sample rate is kept intentionally to preserve the authentic tracker aliasing.

Synth waves will be short 32–64 sample wavetables. The FM bell is being built with a 5:1 modulation ratio and exponential decay, tuned to 261.63 Hz for correct pitch at C-4. It will last roughly 0.72 seconds.

The full script will be a single Python file that generates WAVs, creates the module, loads samples, and writes pattern data via batch JSON files. Each batch will be executed through a subprocess call to FastTracker II. The plan now includes a noise ride or shaker for extra groove, plus three toms played at different relative notes.

The lead melody is being mapped out in a 16th-note piano-roll grid. Theme A spans four bars of sixteen rows, outlining the Am, F, and C chord changes with held notes and grace notes to create a busy, keygen-style line.

Theme A is now fully mapped across four bars of sixteen rows. Harmony will sit a third or sixth below the lead. The brighter C major chorus theme B is also being drafted with its own four-bar phrase.

Pattern 5 will end on G to lead into the break. Pattern 6 will use an Am pedal with arpeggios before rising. A square-wave background arpeggio was considered but dropped in favor of explicit pluck notes.

Portamento slides will be added to the bass on a few chorus transitions using effect 3. The plan is to generate samples first, test a simple beat render, then write the full patterns. A flag compatibility issue was noted: setting loop flags on 16-bit PCM samples might clear the 16-bit flag, though a prior sine test worked.

Calculating the C-4 frequency from a 32-sample loop at 8363 Hz.

Checking FastTracker II's linear period formula. XM note 49 maps to C-4, but the 8363 Hz sample rate may be calibrated for a different reference pitch.

The 1568 Hz peak suggests the sample is being read as 64 8-bit samples rather than 32 int16 samples. That would make the playback rate roughly 50 kHz instead of 8363 Hz.

The 1568 Hz result is about 5.3 times the expected 261 Hz, not a clean sixfold. This suggests FastTracker II may use a different default C-4 reference frequency, possibly 16574 Hz or 33146 Hz.

FastTracker II documentation confirms the C-4 reference frequency is 8363 Hz. The measured 1568 Hz is exactly six times that value, which points to a misalignment in how the tracker interprets the note or octave mapping. The FFT window was also verified as correct.

The RMS amplitude is only 153, far below the expected level for a sine wave at volume 64 and amplitude 16000. Interpreting the 16-bit sample as 8-bit would produce a distorted waveform rather than silence. The low volume suggests the sample may be too short or not looping properly.

The 32-sample loop at 8363 Hz lasts only about 3.8 milliseconds. That brief burst would still produce an RMS near 987, not the observed 153, so the sample is likely being truncated or read as 8-bit instead of 16-bit.

The next step is to test sample flags 16 and 17 to verify whether a 16-bit loop flag is required. The render amplitude was also set to 1.

summary.text:
Confirmed the 261 Hz C-4 tone using flags=17 (16-bit plus loop).

Non-looping 16-bit samples require flags=16. The title is CRC Sunrise, a classic 2000s keygen in major-minor brightness at BPM 142 with speed 4.

Final tempo is 144 BPM at speed 4. The verse progression uses Am, F, C, and G. One bar lasts roughly 1.1 seconds.

The chorus progression is C | G | Am | F. A break uses Dm | G | C | E to lead back to Am.

Bass will play driving 8th-note lines with octave jumps. Drums use a four-on-floor kick, snare on beats two and four, and 16th-hat accents. Kick patterns vary by section: standard bars, a funkier chorus fill, an intro, and a half-time break.

Snare hits on beats four and twelve, with a ghost on ten and occasional fills on beats thirteen through fifteen. Claps layer on those same beats during the chorus. Hats play eighth-note accents on beats zero, two, four, and six, switching to sixteenth-note runs in the chorus. Drums will be generated at 8363 Hz for an authentic crunch. Relative_note values can be used to adjust sample length and pitch.

Drum sample rates are being finalized. 16726 Hz with relative_note +12 would double the kick length, but 8363 Hz is the better choice for authentic low-fi crunch.

Drum samples will be 32 to 256 16-bit loops at 8363 Hz with flags=17.

Bass will be a clean 32-sample loop. The lead synth uses three voices: a 32-sample pulse with a tiny second harmonic, a bandlimited saw with harmonics one through eight, and a triangle wave. An arp pluck is 2048 samples with decay and flags 16. A pad is a 256-sample additive organ loop with flags 17. A bell is a 4096-sample decaying FM note with flags 16.

The bandlimited saw will use a 32-sample loop with harmonics one through eight, each weighted by one over h to avoid aliasing. Pattern effects include volume slides on the pad, vibrato on long lead notes, panning on the hats, and retriggering on the snare fill. The full song will be written as a single Python script with careful mix level adjustments.

XM effect codes are being mapped for the pattern builder. Retrigger is effect 27 (R), vibrato is 4, arpeggio is 0, panning is 8, volume slide is 10, and extended commands are 14.

XM extended effect parameters are now defined: EC4 cuts a note after four ticks, ED2 delays two ticks, EA2 raises volume fine, and E94 retriggers the sample. The ten-channel layout is fixed with Kick on channel zero, Snare and Clap on one, Closed Hat on two, Open Hat and Tom on three, Bass on four, Lead on five, Harmony on six, Arp on seven, Pad on eight, and Bell on nine. Fifteen instruments are mapped from Kick through SoftTriangle. Bass will be written with dead notes and syncopation for a more musical feel.

A helper function will place drum grooves by type. Lead phrases will use note-off and volume variations of 64, 52, and 40 for accents. The module order loops from pattern zero through seven, restarting at two after the final pattern. Pattern seven ends on an E major dominant chord, resolving with a descending melodic run from G#-5 to E-5 and a crash before returning to Am.

Pattern zero is a four-bar intro. It layers pad, hats, and bell motifs before the drum section builds. Pattern one is a sixty-four-row build with full drums, bass, pad, and arp, ending with a snare fill and crash to set up the lead. Patterns two and three are the verse sections in Am, F, C, and G, with the lead melody entering on pattern two and harmony added on pattern three. Pattern four is the sixty-four-row chorus in C, G, Am, and F.

Pattern five is a second sixty-four-row chorus in C, G, Am, and F. It features call-and-response between the lead and bell with maximum energy and sixteenth-note hat runs.

Pattern six is a sixty-four-row break in Dm, G, C, and E. It opens with half-time drums and an arp solo, then rises into a two-bar build with a snare roll.

Pattern seven is the sixty-four-row finale in Am, F, C, and E. Both lead voices play together, ending on an E major dominant chord that resolves back to Am.

The loop will start at pattern two, skipping the intro and build so the first full verse begins immediately.

Drum samples are being shaped for character. The kick will be punchy and short. The snare will be noisy and slightly pitchy like an 808 hybrid. The clap will have multiple transients. Hats will be metallic noise. The open hat will be longer. The crash will be a bright noise sweep. The bass will be fat and slightly square with sub notes. The pulse lead will use a 25% duty cycle for a chip sound. The saw lead will be brighter for the chorus. The pluck will have FM decay for the arp. The pad will use gentle organ harmonics. The bell will sparkle with an FM ratio of two or three point five. The tom will be a sine drop.

A 50% duty square wave will provide the classic 0xy arp effect. A triangle wave will serve as a soft flute-like lead. A reverse cymbal with inverted envelope is being considered for build-ups, and a short noise-plus-sine riser will play at the end of the break. The plan is to generate all samples first, then construct the patterns. Mix analysis will check peak levels, RMS, kick transients, spectral balance, and loop continuity by rendering two full loops and comparing the end of pattern seven to the start of pattern two.

I will write the full composition in a single Python script called `compose.py` that uses FastTracker II batch mode. To avoid bloated base64 JSON, I will generate WAV files and load them directly instead of embedding PCM data. All drum and synth samples will be rendered at 8363 Hz.

FastTracker II ignores WAV header sample rates when calculating pitch, so the 8363 Hz kick and snare will play at their intended frequencies regardless of file metadata. A Python pattern DSL is being drafted to define each channel’s note, instrument, volume, and effect sequence.

A `put` helper is being drafted to place notes, instruments, volumes, and effects into patterns. A `drums_groove` function will generate drum sequences by bar, inserting kicks on beats zero, four, eight, and twelve, plus snare hits on beats four and twelve. Chorus variants will add extra kick accents at beats six and ten.

Clap is assigned to channel three, overlapping with open hat on rows four and twelve. The crash on row zero is placed there instead of the clap. Tom fills occupy channel three during the final four rows of each pattern. Volume zero will mark empty cells.

Default volumes are now fixed for every instrument. Kick is 64, snare 56, clap 50, closed hat 28, open hat 32, crash 48, bass 56, pulse lead 52, saw lead 48, pluck 36, pad 24, bell 40, tom 50, square 20, and triangle 36. The volume column will be reserved for accents and ghost notes only.

The verse lead melody is being notated row by row in the Am F C G progression. Each note is mapped to a sixteen-note row with specific volume levels and a vibrato effect on the E-6 in bar C.

The harmony line is being notated as a quiet third below the lead. It pairs with the verse melody in pattern three.

The chorus lead is being mapped to an anthemic C-G-Am-F progression. It reaches A-6 with a vibrato on the final note.

Sixteenth-note arpeggios are next.

A driving four-note ostinato is being mapped for the arpeggiator across the Am, F, C, and G progressions. Each chord repeats as root-fifth-octave-fifth in sixteenth-note steps at volume 28–36. The pad will hold whole notes on A-3, F-3, C-3, and G-3. Bass lines are being written as eighth-note syncopation with dead notes and alternating root positions.

Bass will retrigger on every eighth note to create a plucked, pumping saw sound. The verse will use eighth-note drive while the break switches to quarter-note sustained notes. A sparse bell hint of the verse melody is being mapped for the intro.

Portamento will be added to the chorus lead, sliding from D-6 to G-6 with effect 3xx. The crash and hat samples will be generated by highpass-filtering white noise, while drum samples will be tanh-saturated for extra punch. All sample generation and pattern construction will be written in a single large Python script.

print("Done.")

def hats_8th(p, bars=4, vol=26, start=0, delay_offbeats=False):
    for bar in range(bars):
        b = start + bar * 16
        for i in range(8):
            row = b + i * 2
            v = vol + 8 if i % 2 == 0 else vol - 4
            v = max(10, min(64, v))
            fx = fp = None
            if delay_offbeats and i % 2 == 1:
                fx, fp = 14, 0xD1  # ED1 note delay 1 tick — slight shuffle
            put(p, row, 2, "F-5", CHAT, v, fx, fp)


def hats_16th(p, bars=4, vol=22, start=0):
    for bar in range(bars):
        b = start + bar * 16
        for i in range(16):
            v = vol
            if i % 4 == 0:
                v = vol + 10
            elif i % 2 == 0:
                v = vol + 4
            else:
                v = vol - 4
            put(p, b + i, 2, "F-5", CHAT, max(8, min(64, v)))


def kicks(p, rows, note="C-4", vol=64):
    for r in rows:
        put(p, r, 0, note, KICK, vol)


def snares(p, rows, vol=56, ins=None):
    ins = ins or SNARE
    for r in rows:
        put(p, r, 1, "C-4", ins, vol)


def open_hats(p, rows, vol=30):
    for r in rows:
        put(p, r, 3, "C-5", OHAT, vol)


def crash(p, row, vol=48, note="C-5"):
    put(p, row, 3, note, CRASH, vol)


# bass line: list of (offset_in_bar, note, vol)
def bass_bar(p, bar_row, events):
    for off, note, vol in events:
        put(p, bar_row + off, 4, note, BASS, vol)


def pad_chord(p, row, note, vol=24):
    put(p, row, 8, note, PAD, vol)


def arp_pattern(p, bar_row, notes4, vol=32, ch=7):
    """8 repetitions of 4-note cell over 16 rows? notes4 played as 16ths twice, then variant.
    notes4 length 4, played 4 times = 16 rows."""
    for i in range(16):
        n = notes4[i % 4]
        v = vol + (6 if i % 4 == 0 else 0)
        put(p, bar_row + i, ch, n, PLUCK, min(64, v))


def lead(p, row, note, ins=PULSE, vol=52, fx=None, fp=None, ch=5):
    put(p, row, ch, note, ins, vol, fx, fp)


def harm(p, row, note, ins=SAW, vol=28, fx=None, fp=None, ch=6):
    put(p, row, ch, note, ins, vol, fx, fp)


def bell(p, row, note, vol=36, ch=9):
    put(p, row, ch, note, BELL, vol)


def off(p, row, ch):
    put(p, row, ch, "OFF")


# Groove templates per bar (16 rows)
KICK_VERSE = [0, 4, 8, 12]
KICK_DRIVE = [0, 4, 6, 8, 12, 14]
KICK_CHORUS = [0, 3, 4, 8, 11, 12]
KICK_HALF = [0, 8]
KICK_BUILD = [0, 4, 8, 10, 12, 14]
SNARE_STD = [4, 12]
SNARE_GHOST_EXTRA = [4, 10, 12]  # 10 ghost handled separately
OHAT_STD = [2, 6, 10, 14]
OHAT_SPARSE = [6, 14]


def groove_verse(p, start=0, bars=4, extra_kick=False):
    for bar in range(bars):
        b = start + bar * 16
        ks = KICK_DRIVE if extra_kick else KICK_VERSE
        for k in ks:
            put(p, b + k, 0, "C-4", KICK, 64 if k % 4 == 0 else 50)
        put(p, b + 4, 1, "C-4", SNARE, 54)
        put(p, b + 12, 1, "C-4", SNARE, 58)
        # ghost
        put(p, b + 10, 1, "C-4", SNARE, 22)
        for h in OHAT_STD:
            put(p, b + h, 3, "C-5", OHAT, 26)


def groove_chorus(p, start=0, bars=4):
    for bar in range(bars):
        b = start + bar * 16
        for k in KICK_CHORUS:
            put(p, b + k, 0, "C-4", KICK, 64 if k in (0, 8) else 48)
        put(p, b + 4, 1, "C-4", SNARE, 58)
        put(p, b + 12, 1, "C-4", SNARE, 60)
        put(p, b + 10, 1, "C-4", SNARE, 24)
        # clap layered on snare beats via ch 3 would fight ohats; put clap on snare channel? can't.
        # use ch 9 sometimes... bells live there. Clap on ch 3 at 4 and 12, ohats on 2,6,10,14.
        put(p, b + 4, 3, "C-4", CLAP, 42)
        put(p, b + 12, 3, "C-4", CLAP, 46)
        put(p, b + 2, 3, "C-5", OHAT, 28)
        put(p, b + 6, 3, "C-5", OHAT, 24)
        put(p, b + 10, 3, "C-5", OHAT, 24)
        put(p, b + 14, 3, "C-5", OHAT, 26)


def fill_toms(p, start_row=60):
    """Last 4 rows tom/snare fill. Overwrites ch 0,1,3."""
    put(p, start_row + 0, 0, "C-4", KICK, 50)
    put(p, start_row + 0, 3, "A-4", TOM, 48)
    put(p, start_row + 1, 3, "F-4", TOM, 50)
    put(p, start_row + 2, 1, "C-4", SNARE, 40)
    put(p, start_row + 2, 3, "D-4", TOM, 52)
    put(p, start_row + 3, 0, "C-4", KICK, 64)
    put(p, start_row + 3, 1, "C-4", SNARE, 60)
    put(p, start_row + 3, 3, "C-5", CRASH, 40)

The keygen tune requirements are now clear.

The intro bar is too quiet. The pad and hats are muted by low volume and small sample peaks. A crash or kick on the first beat will add presence.

The bass is too loud and creates a jarring energy jump at bar 3. Drums and leads need to be louder, while the bass should be quieter and punchier. The mix will be brighter, with wider stereo panning and clearer separation between instruments.

A soft kick will open the intro to fill the silence. Extreme panning is planned for every instrument, from 20 to 220. Arp notes will ping-pong across the stereo field via effect 8. The volume column overrides each sample's default amplitude.

The volume column overrides each sample's default amplitude. Raising the sample volume alone will not fix the mix. The lead and bass patterns need higher explicit volume values. The bass sample itself is too loud in the low frequencies. It needs a lower peak and less sub. The lead sample should be brighter. The drum samples should be punchier.

The bass will be raised one octave to A-2 and F-2. This removes low-frequency rumble and fits the classic chip-bass keygen style. The intro will open with a soft kick at volume 40 on beats 0 and 8, plus a brighter bell motif that becomes the hook. The track stays within ten channels.

The lead will be set to full volume at 64, while the bass drops to 40–48. The kick stays punchy, the snare gets louder and snappier, and the hats are raised. The pulse and pluck samples will be brighter with sharper attacks, and the pad will lose its fundamental tone for a cleaner sound. Note frequencies were verified against XM ranges.

Channel 3 is being double-assigned in the groove_chorus pattern. The crash on row 0 and the ohats on rows 2, 6, 10, and 14 would collide with the clap on rows 4 and 12. This overlap needs to be resolved.

Tom fills on channels 0, 1, and 3 will not clash with the hat pattern because hats occupy channel 2. Portamento and pad volume slides will add melodic interest. The sample rebuilds are now underway.

The tempo may rise to 150 BPM for more keygen energy. The pulse lead will be brighter, either by narrowing the duty cycle or adding harmonics. The pluck decay shortens at higher arps, which suits the upper range but risks overlap at low notes. Pattern 7 and pattern 2 were checked for a clean loop boundary.

The loop boundary at order position 2 is confirmed clean. Instruments retrigger properly on the next cycle, and one-shot bells remain unaffected.

The bass sample will be shaped with a highpass filter to suppress the first harmonic and prevent boom at the raised octave.

A chip-style echo effect was considered but skipped in favor of other improvements.

The next step is to rebuild the samples and update the composition script.

The snare decay is being cut from 0.38 seconds to 0.22 seconds for a tighter keygen feel. The kick will be made clickier for small speakers. The intro will open with a crash, soft kicks on beats zero and eight, and a bell hook playing E-5, A-5, G-5, E-5. Bass will enter at bar one instead of bar three so the first 1.1 seconds are not empty.

A closed hat will play on every sixteenth note from the start of pattern one. The script will be patched in place rather than regenerated entirely. The bass notes are being mapped to their exact higher-octave equivalents.

The bass will be raised one full octave after all. The Am and C chord patterns are being mapped to the new higher notes. Note-cuts on the bass will add punch instead of letting it drone continuously.

sr = 44100
n = len(raw)
dur = n/sr

print(f'rms L {np.sqrt(np.mean(raw[:,0]**2)):.0f} R {np.sqrt(np.mean(raw[:,1]**2)):.0f}')

print(f'stereo corr {np.corrcoef(raw[:,0], raw[:,1])[0,1]:.3f}')

    sl = raw[s:e]

    pk = np.max(np.abs(sl))
    mono = sl.mean(1)
    spec = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(mono * np.hanning(len(mono))))
    freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(mono), 1/sr)
    def band(a,b):

        return float(np.mean(spec[m])) if np.any(m) else 0
    print(f'P{i} rms={rms:6.0f} pk={pk:6.0f}  lo={band(30,150):8.0f} mid={band(200,2500):8.0f} hi={band(2500,10000):8.0f}')

silent=0; run=0; maxrun=0

The tune will begin immediately with no silence.

The stereo mix is slightly wider but still centered. Peak amplitude is 45% with no clipping. The intro carries energy. Bass and low frequencies dominate the mix. The lead instrument is too quiet relative to the bass. The finale finally shows the lead at high frequencies. The build pattern lacks high harmonics.

Bass volume will drop to 32–38 and pattern volumes to 36. The bass sample will be thinned into a chip-like square to cut rumble. Pluck and lead samples will be boosted so the lead becomes the star instrument.

The lead must be bright and prominent. The bass will become a 50% square wave at A-2 with a weaker fundamental to preserve odd harmonics on small speakers. The verse FFT lacks the lead melody at E-5 and A-5, so the lead is buried. Estimating lead contribution without muting channels is difficult.

Exact channel volumes are now set. Bass drops to 28–36. Pad, arps, and harmony fall to 18–22, 28–32, and 28. Kick and snare stay at 56–64 and 50–58. Lead holds at 64. A second lead doubling is being considered.

Bass note volumes will drop from 34–46 to 24–34. Pad volumes fall from 30–32 to 20. Arp sparkle stays at 32–38. The lead needs more high-frequency presence.

The lead notes may be missing due to a bug in pattern 2 channel 5. Linear interpolation could also be damping the pulse harmonics. I will check those cells and try rendering a short section to isolate the problem.

The verse mix is solid. The E-5 note at 661 Hz stands out as the top peak, confirming the melody is the star.

The chorus peaks at E-6 (1317 Hz) as an anthemic lead. The track runs 16 instruments, 8 patterns, and 10 channels in real XM. Dynamics build from quiet intro through verse and finale. The break modulates through Dm G C E for a satisfying harmonic journey. The loop from E to Am is tight. Thirty-five seconds with the verse loop is a solid keygen length. The square bubble arpeggiator, vibrato on long notes, and ping-pong arps add character. Pattern 1’s lower high-frequency level may feel slightly subdued compared to the lead-heavy intro, but the track is otherwise complete.
